title: Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors
claim: Different task objectives define distinct minima in a shared parameter space, so transfer strategies steer optimization toward compromise solutions or risk poor minima.
layout: Single panel, three overlapping loss basins left-center-right, curved warm-start arrow, bottom legend
description: A single wide panel shows a 2-D loss landscape drawn as contour ellipses. A red basin on the left is labeled Node Classification (NC), with a red star at its L_NC minimum. A blue basin on the right is labeled Link Prediction (LP), with a blue star at its L_LP minimum. A green basin overlaps both at the bottom center. It holds a purple star for the joint-loss minimum and an orange star for the MV-loss minimum. Gray dots scattered near the center mark other local minima. A thick orange arrow labeled Warm Start Path curves over the top from the NC minimum to the LP basin. Dashed contours and soft color gradients fill the basins. A legend along the bottom maps the star and dot symbols to their meanings. The eye goes first to the orange arc, then to the stars.
caption: Cross-task transfer as optimization in a shared parameter space. For a fixed GNN/GT architecture, NC and LP correspond to different losses over the same parameters, yielding distinct (possibly incompatible) minima. Warm start initializes the target training near a source-task solution, while MV and Joint couple objectives to steer optimization toward solutions that perform well on both tasks; other local minima illustrate potential negative transfer.
abstract: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find that transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC $\to$ LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP $\to$ NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP $\to$ NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting that LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.
